prize_parts.citation: for a visionary, densely patterned body of prose and poetry in which memory, the body and dream are built into a metaphysical architecture of the novel

statement.case_for: I keep Cărtărescu first on the common criteria. The voice is distinctive: from public knowledge of Blinding and Solenoid, the prose is dense, hallucinatory and patterned, and it draws on poetic, fantastic and encyclopedic registers. The formal and linguistic ambition is high, and the imaginative depth is sustained over a large scale rather than confined to one book. The ballot summary and public knowledge also indicate a long career across poetry and fiction with a coherent imaginative world, which supports a whole-oeuvre citation that is anchored in the Romanian-language corpus and not only in the best-known novels. I base this on literary grounds alone and not on the number of colleagues who ranked him first. Agreement in the openings does not test the argument, so the points below are the ones that should be tested.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that my judgment of a very dense Romanian prose style rests on translations and public knowledge, not on direct reading or independent verification. The length and recursiveness of the large novels could mean that the method repeats more than it deepens in the later work. The poetry and early work, which a whole-oeuvre citation would cover, are less well known abroad and less visible in the supplied entry. If the later novels extend the project less than the central ones do, the claim to sustained quality weakens, and a poet with a more clearly established formal transformation of a language, such as Adonis, would become the stronger case.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for the scale, formal ambition and unmistakable voice of the Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid. She also notes that the late work may be repetitive or over-extended in places, and that the poetry and early work are less known to her.
responses.response: I agree that this reservation is the one that matters most, and I do not think it can be settled by pointing to the scale of the books. Some recursiveness is part of the method, since the same motifs of memory, body and cosmos return at larger scale. The real question is whether Solenoid and the later work transform those motifs or only repeat them. I have not read the whole corpus and cannot answer that for the committee. I would therefore want the argument for the citation to rest on the poetry and the novels together, not on one trilogy. I would also treat the poetry as a test of that unity, not as decoration, and I share her uncertainty about how well it is known.

responses.point: Sward ranks Adonis second for a decades-long renewal of Arabic poetic language through verse and critical prose. She stresses that much of the achievement lies in Arabic sound and metre, which translation conveys only partly, and that the main questions are timing and how the essays and poetry weigh against each other.
responses.response: I take this as the strongest competing case, and I rank Adonis third in my opening, close to second. I agree that the formal and linguistic achievement is major and that the oeuvre is established. I would qualify two points. Timing and age are not literary arguments and should not decide between the two. The difficulty she describes, that sound and metre lose most in translation, applies to my own judgment of him as much as to hers. It means any committee view of Adonis depends on competence in Arabic that the committee does not fully have internally. The regional expert reports adopted as policy from 2022, for Asian and African literature, may bear on this, although I do not assume they cover every language question. If that competence cannot be secured, I think the Cărtărescu case is somewhat better supported by the evidence we can actually weigh, while the Adonis case remains very serious.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Zurita third and treats the landscape-scale and sky-writing works as extensions of the poems, not a separate field. He values the poetic form over documentary witness, and he flags the excess and encyclopedic density of Cărtărescu as something the committee may weigh differently.
responses.response: On Zurita I largely agree and would go further. For a citation under Nobel's will, the printed sequences, Purgatory and Anteparadise, must carry the case, and the public works can only be context. If the claim depends on the installations, it becomes harder to defend as literary achievement. On the density of Cărtărescu, I think the objection is fair and not a matter of taste alone. Encyclopedic excess is part of the voice, but it is a risk to the claim of sustained quality if it becomes mannered. I would ask whether the density carries imaginative necessity from book to book. I do not think it should be dismissed in advance, and I do not claim to have settled it. I keep Zurita as an alternative and not as a first choice because his cumulative, visually structured poems are the hardest of the leading cases to judge in translation.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu first on voice and imaginative depth, and notes that his poetry and early work are less covered. She ranks Carson third and raises doubts about how hybrid and visual works fit the will's phrase 'literary works'.
responses.response: I share her doubt about Carson and have ranked her fourth for similar reasons. It is unclear how much of her achievement rests on the books as objects and how much on the text, and some of her work is scholarly or translational, which complicates defining the core oeuvre. Her point about the thinner coverage of Cărtărescu's poetry also applies to my own case, as noted above. I would add that this is a reason to define the citation carefully, naming prose and poetry, and not to assume the poetry is covered just because it appears on the ballot.

uncertainties: My assessment of Cărtărescu's prose rhythm and density rests on public knowledge and translated reception. I have not read the texts or independently verified sources, and the effect of the Romanian original in translation is hard to judge.
Corpus coverage is uneven: the poetry and early work are less known abroad than the major novels, so the strength of a whole-oeuvre citation covering both is not established.
It is unresolved whether the later large novels extend or repeat the central project, which bears on sustained quality.

Adonis and Zurita depend on Arabic and Spanish poetic language, which translation conveys only partly. The committee's own competence for Arabic is uncertain, and I am not sure how far regional expert input can close that gap.
The weight of Zurita's landscape-scale and public works in a literary judgment remains open.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My scholarly work on modern poetry, exile literature, the fragment and Celan is context and not evidence of a preference for any candidate. The listed professional ties (Horace Engdahl, Daniel Birnbaum and the Kris circle) do not connect to any shortlisted writer in the supplied profile.
